lead: Jowl filler is the use of injectable dermal filler in the pre-jowl, marionette and lower-face areas to restore lost volume and smooth the line of the jaw. People choose it to soften the sagging that blurs the jawline with age, so the lower face looks firmer and the jaw looks more continuous and defined.

Dermal fillers are substances injected into connective tissue; hyaluronic acid is among the most common, and fillers are used for wrinkles, volume loss and shaping of the lips, cheeks and jawline.[1] Hyaluronic acid fillers are typically cross-linked, other materials include poly-L-lactic acid, which gradually stimulates the body's own collagen, as well as PMMA and collagen.[1] Most wrinkle fillers are temporary because the body breaks them down, and some people return for repeat treatments.[1]

Common side effects include bruising, redness, pain and itching; rare vascular complications can cause permanent vision loss or skin necrosis.[1] Clinical research specific to jowls is small: one registered trial of fillers for jowl improvement enrolled 16 participants.[2]

angle.text: Filler adds volume along the pre-jowl and jaw so the contour looks straighter and firmer. People use it to tidy the jawline without surgery.

infobox: Temporary for most fillers (about six months is cited for wrinkle fillers)[1]

paras: Fillers are used to correct folds, restore volume lost with age and contour areas such as the jawline.[1] Filler materials include hyaluronic acid, poly-L-lactic acid, PMMA, collagen and autologous fat.[1] Poly-L-lactic acid does not give immediate volume but gradually stimulates collagen production.[1]

Reference works state that most wrinkle fillers are temporary because the body breaks them down, with an effect cited as lasting about six months, and results depend on skin health, the provider and the product; exercise and physically demanding work are said to shorten longevity.[1]

Reported adverse effects include bruising, redness, pain, itching, infection, allergic reaction, lumps and scarring. Embolisation into eye arteries can cause usually permanent vision loss, and delayed skin necrosis can follow vascular events.[1] In the US fillers are regulated as medical devices and must be prescribed and administered by a provider; in the UK and EEA they are CE-marked non-prescription devices that licensed practitioners can inject.[1]

A registered clinical study, Jowl Improvement With Injectable Fillers, was completed in 2020 with 16 participants.[2] A phase 3 trial of an injectable material for wrinkle correction listing jowls as a condition was registered in 2007 and withdrawn.[3] No results are summarised in the registry records.

card.summary: Filler placed along the pre-jowl and marionette lines to smooth the lower face; established aesthetic medicine with thin jowl-specific trial data.
card.note: Rare vascular complications can cause permanent harm.

quick.overview:
Jowl filler is the use of injectable dermal filler, most often hyaluronic acid, to fill the hollow in front of the jowl and the marionette area so the jaw line looks smoother.

It is a mainstream aesthetic procedure; trials focused on jowls are few and small.
quick.mechanism: The filler adds volume under the skin. Hyaluronic acid products are usually cross-linked for stability [1].
quick.risks: Bruising and redness are common. Embolisation can cause blindness or skin necrosis in rare cases [1]. Fillers are regulated as medical devices [1].
